I am 59 years old. I never went to school, not one day. My father put me in the fields when I was 14, and I have farmed my whole life. My land is 10.7 mu, all one plot near the village. I grow winter wheat and summer corn on the same piece, one after another, every year. My wife and I do the work. My son and daughter-in-law work in a factory in the county town, so they are not here for the farming.

I do not read books, and I do not trust outsiders who tell me what to do. I watch my neighbors. If Old Zhang puts more fertilizer and his corn grows taller, I put more too. If someone tries a new seed and it fails, I never touch that seed again. Last year, fertilizer was expensive, but the corn price was okay, so I did not cut back. I would rather spend the money on fertilizer than lose half my harvest. A bad harvest means we go hungry. Wasting some fertilizer is just money out of pocket.

For wheat: After we harvest corn in October, I rotary till the field. I spread one big bag of compound fertilizer on each mu — 100 jin bags, the kind from the dealer with three numbers on the front. Then I sow wheat seed, the improved kind that everyone in the village uses, about 20 jin per mu. Before winter sets in, I irrigate once from my well so the little plants do not freeze dry. In spring, when the wheat turns green, I spread 50 jin of urea on each mu. I irrigate two more times: once when it shoots up, and once when the heads come out. That is three times total. For spraying, I do it twice: once early for the weeds, and once later if I see insects on the leaves. If the weather does not play tricks, I should get about 900 jin per mu.

For corn: In June, the day after we cut the wheat, I sow hybrid corn seed right into the stubble without plowing. Time is short — if you wait too long, the season is gone. I plant about 4 to 5 jin of seed per mu. At sowing, I put one big bag of compound fertilizer in the row, same as wheat, 100 jin per mu. Then when the corn is knee-high, I side-dress another 50 jin of urea per mu. Corn grows fast and needs food. I irrigate twice: once when it is small if the rain does not come, and once at big trumpet when the tassels are coming out. I spray twice: herbicide right after sowing, and insecticide once when the corn borers show up. Good corn should give me about 1,100 jin per mu.

This is my plan. I know the costs — the compound fertilizer, the urea, the diesel for the pump, the seed, the medicine. It all adds up. But I have no choice. I must put enough food in the soil, or the soil will give me nothing back. I have done it this way for many years, and it has kept us fed.
